questions.question_text:
Does $P=6n$ represent direct variation?
If so, state the constant of variation.

options.why: Confused $y=kx$ with $y=k/x$ and took the reciprocal of the coefficient.
Mistook the direct-variation form $y=kx$ for the inverse form $y=k/x$.
Identified the variable $n$ itself as the constant of variation instead of its coefficient.

questions.solution_text:
$P=6n$ is in the form $y=kx$, so this is direct variation.
Constant of variation: $k=6$

options.text: No, because of the added constant $18$

options.why: Ignored the added constant term and read $k$ straight off the coefficient of $m$.

options.text: No, because $m$ is multiplied by a coefficient
options.why: Treated any multiplication by a variable as disqualifying, when a coefficient alone is fine for direct variation.
Added the constant term to the coefficient instead of checking whether the constant term should be zero.

questions.solution_text:
$C=18+5m$ has a constant term $18$ added on, so it is not in the form $y=kx$.
This is not direct variation.

options.text: No, because $x$ is in the denominator, not multiplied by a constant

options.why: Read the numerator as the constant of variation without checking whether $x$ is multiplied or divided.
Took the reciprocal of the numerator, confusing the direct and inverse variation forms.

options.text: No, because $10$ is too large to be a constant of variation
options.why: Invented a size restriction on $k$ that doesn't exist — any nonzero value can be a constant of variation.

questions.solution_text:
$y=\dfrac{10}{x}$ has $x$ in the denominator instead of being multiplied by a constant, so it is not in the form $y=kx$.
This is not direct variation.

questions.question_text:
Does $y=\dfrac{x}{8}$ represent direct variation?
If so, state the constant of variation.

options.why: Used the divisor $8$ as the coefficient instead of rewriting division by $8$ as multiplication by $1/8$.
Mistook division by a constant for division by the variable.
Identified the variable $x$ as the constant of variation instead of its coefficient.

questions.solution_text:
$y=\dfrac{x}{8}$ can be written $y=\dfrac{1}{8}x$, which matches the form $y=kx$, so this is direct variation.
Constant of variation: $k=\dfrac{1}{8}$

questions.question_text:
A vending machine sells identical bottles of water at a fixed price each.
Is the total amount spent directly proportional to the number of bottles bought?
Explain.

options.text: Yes, because doubling the number of bottles doubles the total amount spent
No, because the price could change over time
options.why: Introduced a condition (a changing price) that isn't stated in the scenario.

options.text: No, because you also have to pay for the machine itself
options.why: Invented an extra fixed cost that the scenario never mentions.

options.text: Yes, because doubling the number of bottles halves the total amount spent
options.why: Applied the inverse-proportion scaling rule instead of multiplying the cost by the same factor as the number of bottles.

questions.solution_text:
Doubling the number of bottles bought doubles the total amount spent, since the cost is always the price per bottle multiplied by the number of bottles.
This is direct variation.

questions.question_text:
A café charges a fixed price per coffee.
Buying $6$ coffees costs $\$27$ in total.
The total cost $C$ is directly proportional to the number of coffees $n$.
Find the constant of variation.

options.why: Multiplied $27$ by $6$ instead of dividing to find the price per coffee.
Divided $6$ by $27$, taking the reciprocal of the correct ratio, then rounded $2/9$ to two decimal places.
Subtracted the number of coffees from the total cost instead of dividing.

questions.question_text:
$y \propto x$, and $y=45$ when $x=9$.
Find the constant of variation $k$.

options.why: Divided $x$ by $y$ instead of $y$ by $x$, finding the reciprocal of $k$.
Subtracted $x$ from $y$ instead of dividing.
Multiplied $y$ and $x$ together instead of dividing.

questions.question_text:
Does $m=-\dfrac{5n}{8}$ represent direct variation?
If so, state the constant of variation.

options.text: No, because the coefficient is negative
options.why: Wrongly assumed the constant of variation must be positive.
Dropped the negative sign from the coefficient.
Took the reciprocal of the coefficient instead of reading the multiplier of $n$.

questions.solution_text:
$m=-\dfrac{5n}{8}$ can be written $m=-\dfrac{5}{8}n$, which matches the form $y=kx$, so this is direct variation.
Constant of variation: $k=-\dfrac{5}{8}$
